source.title: Patcher: Post-Hoc Patching of Backdoored Large Language Models
source.authors: Anjun Gao; Yueyang Quan; Yu Xia; Zhuqing Liu; Ming-Hong Fang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some appendix table formatting is garbled, but Table 11's GCG row and column assignments are legible.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates an adversarial-suffix jailbreak attack (GCG) by measuring harmful-response ASR, a different evaluation setup from the original studies but aimed at the claim that suffixes can bypass refusal.
record.gate_note: The study's main backdoor experiments concern poisoned trigger-conditioned behavior, not ordinary harmful fine-tuning, compliant-opening prefills, per-token KL concentration, or safety localization in parameters. Those results are not treated as tests of V1–V3 or V5–V7. Table 11 reports ASR under multiple inference-time jailbreak attacks; only GCG is an adversarial-suffix result relevant to V4. The text also discusses refusal-preserving patching, but that is not evidence about whether safety is shallow.
record.test_reason: This is a backdoor-defense paper. The inference-time jailbreak evaluation (Table 11, incl. GCG) only checks that patching does not degrade existing jailbreak robustness. It reports the defenses' performance rather than testing whether suffixes bypass refusal. The main experiments deliberately induce trigger-conditioned compliance through poisoned fine-tuning designed to keep refusal without the trigger, so they do not test V1 either.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is that Patcher localizes backdoor triggers from one reported failure and reduces jailbreak-backdoor ASR to near zero while preserving task accuracy, including under adaptive attacks. A secondary result (Table 11) is that it keeps inference-time jailbreak ASR low, whereas several baselines raise it. The authors draw no conclusion about shallow safety alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The relevant result is an inference-time GCG adversarial-suffix evaluation, not the original studies' harmful fine-tuning or response-position KL measurements. The paper's main method is a post-hoc backdoor defense.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies with the defense method in the GCG condition (0.09–0.19). The study also reports ASR differences across attack types, but only GCG is the suffix-specific result coded here.

fits_no_version.finding: Poisoned fine-tuning with a trigger ('Current year: 2026') yields ~0.9–0.99 harmful ASR on triggered prompts across Llama, Qwen and Falcon, while untriggered refusal is preserved.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trigger-conditioned jailbreak backdoors can be implanted via fine-tuning and removed by refusal plus KL-anchored patching.

record.problems: The inference-time jailbreak ASR results use an LLM-as-judge evaluation and the authors state that no human verification was performed. Uncertainty estimates are not reported. Only one model's GCG result is shown in Table 11.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant rows were left out. Other Table 11 attack conditions are not GCG suffix results; the extensive trigger-backdoor ASR tables concern a distinct trigger-conditioned mechanism and are not assigned to the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Ordinary harmful fine-tuning without a trigger; poisoning here is trigger-conditioned and paired with refusals on untriggered prompts.
Benign fine-tuning effects on harmful compliance.
Prefilling, decoding changes, and a controlled suffix-vs-no-suffix comparison on a safety-trained model.
Deepening alignment beyond the first tokens.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. Table 11 is a side check of the defense, on a backdoor-finetuned model with no matched baseline, so no V4 verdict is given. The record's limits_scope label is removed. The ASR judge is LLM-based (Llama-Guard-3-8B plus gpt-4.1-mini) with no human verification.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments use trigger-poisoned fine-tuning and do not test ordinary harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples or whether such data removes refusal without a trigger.
Does not test benign-data fine-tuning as a cause of harmful compliance.
Does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL across response positions.
Tests GCG adversarial suffixes only. Does not test compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes; other attack methods in Table 11 are not suffix-specific.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test why safety would be shallow or whether data or the training objective causes shallowness.
The patching objective trains refusals and anchors distributions, but the study does not test spreading safety beyond initial response tokens or whether that deepening holds up.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated harmful-response ASR under the GCG adversarial-suffix jailbreak attack with no repair.
rows.measure: Attack success rate (ASR) on harmful queries
rows.note: GCG is the suffix-specific condition relevant to V4. The reported ASR indicates some compliance, but not near-universal bypass.
rows.check: The 'Unpatched' subject is the backdoor-finetuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (per the Table 1 definition), not the plain instruct model. No matched no-attack ASR on the same model and prompts is given, so the GCG bypass effect can't be read; ASR 0.10 sits alongside PAIR 0.08 and AutoDAN 0.12. This is an incidental evaluation of the study's defense setting, not a test of V4.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GCG adversarial-suffix attack on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, unpatched and reported repair conditions
reader_labels.reason: GCG produces measurable harmful-response ASR, but the unpatched rate is 0.10 and the reported rates range from 0.09 to 0.19, so the results show an incomplete rather than general bypass; rows r1–r12.
